cards.title: Variables and data types
cards.summary: A variable is a named box that holds a value; the value's type decides what you can do with it.

levels.beginner: A variable is a name that points at a value, like price = 20. Every value has a type: a number, text called a string, true or false called a boolean, or a list. The type decides what makes sense: you can add two numbers, but adding a number to text glues them together instead.
levels.intermediate: In JavaScript, let makes a variable you can reassign and const makes one you cannot. Numbers and strings are copied when you assign them, but objects and arrays are shared: two names can point at the same list, so a change made through one shows through the other. typeof tells you a value's type while the program runs.
levels.expert: A type is a contract about which operations are valid. Static type systems such as TypeScript and Dart check that contract before the program runs; dynamic ones such as JavaScript and Python check it while it runs, and JavaScript also converts types on its own, so "5" + 1 is "51" while "5" - 1 is 4. JavaScript numbers are binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, which is why money is best kept in whole cents.

cards.analogy: A variable is like a labelled jar in a kitchen: the label is the name, what is inside is the value, and whether it holds flour or water is the type, which decides what you can do with it.

example.explain: It checks three types (number, string, boolean), shows that "5" + 1 joins into "51" while "5" - 1 is 4, that a shared list seen through a second name grows to 3 items, and that 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false.

quiz.q: What type is the value "hello"?
quiz.a: A string, which is text.

quiz.q: Two names point at the same array and you push through one. Does the other see it?
quiz.a: Yes. Arrays are shared, so both names see the change.

quiz.q: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3 in JavaScript?
quiz.a: Numbers are binary floating point, which cannot store 0.1 exactly. Keep money in whole cents.

misconceptions: const does not freeze a value: it only stops the name being reassigned, and the array or object it holds can still change.

cards.title: Loops and iteration
cards.summary: A loop repeats the same steps for each item, or until a condition is met.

levels.beginner: A loop repeats the same steps for each item, or until a condition is met. A for loop counts through things; a while loop keeps going while something is still true. Every loop needs a way to stop, or it runs forever.
levels.intermediate: Loop over an array with for...of and keep a running total in a variable outside the loop. Watch the boundaries: starting at 0 and stopping before the length visits every item once and avoids the classic off-by-one error. break leaves a loop early and continue skips to the next round.
levels.expert: Reason about a loop with an invariant: a statement that is true before and after every round, such as "total is the sum of the items seen so far". If the invariant holds and the loop ends, the loop is correct. The work done is the number of rounds times the cost of one round, which is where Big-O comes from.

cards.analogy: A loop is like dealing cards around a table: the same move, one player at a time, until the deck is empty.

formula.name: Sum of the first n whole numbers
formula.spoken: the sum of 1 to n equals n times n plus 1, divided by 2

variables.unit: a whole number, zero or more

formula.assumptions: n is a whole number of zero or more.

example.explain: A for loop adds 1 to 100 and gets 5050, the same as the formula 100 times 101 divided by 2.

quiz.q: What must every loop have so it does not run forever?
quiz.a: A condition that eventually becomes false, or a break.

quiz.q: A loop runs i from 0 while i < length. How many items does it visit?
quiz.a: Exactly length items, from index 0 to length minus 1.

quiz.q: What is 1 + 2 + … + 10?
quiz.a: 55, from 10 times 11 divided by 2.

misconceptions: Stopping at i <= length visits one item too many: the last index is length minus 1.

cards.title: Functions and scope
cards.summary: A function is a named recipe: inputs in, steps, a result out.

levels.beginner: A function is a named recipe: you give it inputs, it does its steps and hands back a result. Write the steps once, call the function many times, and each piece of the program stays short and easy to check.
levels.intermediate: Parameters are the inputs a function declares; arguments are the values you pass when you call it. return sends the result back and ends the function. Scope is where a name can be seen: a variable made inside a function is invisible outside it, which keeps functions from tripping over each other.
levels.expert: A closure is a function that keeps the variables of the place where it was made, even after that code has finished running, which gives private state without a class. A pure function, whose result depends only on its inputs and which changes nothing outside itself, is the easiest kind to test, cache and run in parallel.

cards.analogy: A function is like a coffee machine: put in beans and water, press the button and coffee comes out; you don't need to know what happens inside to use it.

example.explain: makeCounter returns a closure with its own private count: the first counter reaches 3 after three calls, a second counter starts again at 1, and count itself is not visible outside, so its type there is undefined.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
quiz.a: A parameter is the name in the function's definition; an argument is the value passed when it is called.

quiz.q: Can code outside a function read a variable declared with let inside it?
quiz.a: No. It is local to the function's scope.

quiz.q: What does a closure remember?
quiz.a: The variables of the place where it was made, even after that code finished running.

misconceptions: A function that changes a shared variable is not pure, even if it returns the right answer.

cards.title: Unit testing
cards.summary: A test is a small program that checks another program and fails loudly when it breaks.

levels.beginner: A test is a small program that checks another program: it runs a function with known inputs and compares the answer with the one you expect. If someone breaks the function later, the test fails and says so right away.
levels.intermediate: A good unit test is fast, independent and gives the same answer every run: no network, no clock and no randomness unless it is seeded. Arrange the inputs, act by calling the code, assert the result. Write the failing test first to prove it can catch the bug, then fix the code until it passes.
levels.expert: Unit tests check pieces, integration tests check pieces together, and end-to-end tests check the real path a user takes. Property-based tests state an invariant, such as "sorting twice gives the same as sorting once", and try many generated inputs. A test that can never fail proves nothing, so break the code on purpose and make sure a test notices.

cards.analogy: A test is like a smoke alarm: quiet while everything is fine, loud the moment something burns, and only worth having once you have checked that it really goes off.

example.explain: Two checks on an add function both pass, and the same check catches a broken version that subtracts, so caught is true.

quiz.q: What three steps make up a typical unit test?
quiz.a: Arrange the inputs, act by calling the code, assert the result.

quiz.q: Why write the failing test before the fix?
quiz.a: To prove the test can actually catch the bug.

quiz.q: Why should a unit test avoid the network?
quiz.a: So it is fast and gives the same answer every run.

misconceptions: Full coverage does not mean correct: a line can run in a test without any assertion checking its result.

cards.title: Big-O notation
cards.summary: Big-O describes how the work grows when the input grows.

levels.beginner: Big-O describes how the work grows when the input grows. O(n) means twice the data takes about twice the time; O(1) means the time stays the same however much data there is; O(n²) means twice the data takes about four times as long.
levels.intermediate: Count the steps that grow with the input and keep only the fastest-growing term, dropping constants: 3n + 7 is O(n), and two nested loops over n items are O(n²). Binary search halves what is left on every step, so on a sorted list it needs at most the floor of log₂ n, plus 1, comparisons: 10 for a thousand items and 20 for a million.
levels.expert: Formally, f(n) is O(g(n)) when there are constants c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀: an upper bound. Big-Omega is the matching lower bound, and Big-Theta means both. Big-O hides constants and assumes large inputs, so for small n a simple O(n²) method can beat an O(n log n) one; memory use, worst versus average case, and amortized cost, like an array that doubles when it is full, each need stating on their own.

cards.analogy: Big-O is like asking how a trip's time grows with distance rather than how long today's drive took: walking, driving and flying grow at different rates whatever the traffic.

formula.name: Binary search, worst case
formula.expression: comparisons(n) = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1
formula.spoken: the worst-case number of comparisons for binary search is the floor of log base 2 of n, plus 1

variables.meaning: the number of items in the sorted list

formula.assumptions: The list is sorted, and each comparison rules out half of what is left.

example.explain: Binary search for a missing value, its worst case, takes 10 comparisons on 1000 sorted items and 20 on a million, where checking every item would take 1000.

quiz.q: Two nested loops each run over n items. What is the Big-O?
quiz.a: O(n²): n rounds of n steps.

quiz.q: What is 5n + 100 in Big-O?
quiz.a: O(n). Constants and smaller terms are dropped.

quiz.q: At most how many comparisons does binary search need for 1,000 sorted items?
quiz.a: 10, because the floor of log₂ 1000 is 9, plus 1.

misconceptions: O(n) is not always faster than O(n²): Big-O says how time grows, not how long a particular small input takes.

cards.title: Recursion
cards.summary: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of it.

levels.beginner: Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until the problem is so small the answer is obvious. That obvious case is the base case, and without it the function never stops.
levels.intermediate: Every recursive function needs a base case that answers directly and a recursive case that moves toward it: factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), with factorial(1) = 1. Each call waits on the call stack until the one below it returns, so factorial(n) goes n calls deep. Naive Fibonacci calls itself twice per step and makes 2·F(n+1) − 1 calls, which explodes; remembering answers already worked out, called memoization, cuts that to about n.
levels.expert: Model the cost with a recurrence: naive Fibonacci's calls follow C(n) = C(n − 1) + C(n − 2) + 1, whose solution 2·F(n+1) − 1 grows exponentially, while divide and conquer such as merge sort's T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives O(n log n). The call stack is limited, and JavaScript engines throw a RangeError after some thousands of frames depending on the engine, so very deep recursion should become a loop with an explicit stack; JavaScript does not reliably remove tail calls.

cards.analogy: Recursion is like Russian nesting dolls: to reach the smallest doll you open a doll, then do the same thing to the doll inside, until you reach one that does not open.

formula.name: Calls made by naive Fibonacci
formula.expression: calls(n) = 2·F(n+1) − 1, with F(1) = F(2) = 1
formula.spoken: naive Fibonacci of n makes 2 times the Fibonacci number n plus 1, minus 1, calls

variables.unit: a whole number, zero or more

formula.assumptions: fib(0) and fib(1) are base cases that return without calling again. Depth is separate: factorial(n) is n calls deep for n of 1 or more.

example.explain: Naive fib(10) returns 55 but takes 177 calls; factorial(5) returns 120 at a depth of 5 calls.

quiz.q: What two parts does every recursive function need?
quiz.a: A base case that answers directly, and a recursive case that moves toward it.

quiz.q: How many calls deep does factorial(6) go?
quiz.a: 6 calls deep, from factorial 6 down to factorial 1.

quiz.q: How many calls does naive fib(5) make?
quiz.a: 15, which is 2 times F(6), 8, minus 1.

misconceptions: Recursion is not always slower than a loop, but naive recursion that repeats the same subproblem can be exponentially slower.

cards.title: Hash maps
cards.summary: A hash map finds a value straight from its key, without searching.

levels.beginner: A hash map stores pairs: a key and its value, like a word and its meaning. You find a value straight from its key, without searching the whole collection, so looking things up stays fast even with millions of entries.
levels.intermediate: A hash function turns each key into a number that picks a bucket, so lookups, inserts and deletes take O(1) time on average. Two keys can land in the same bucket, a collision; the map keeps both and compares the keys to tell them apart. In JavaScript use a Map, in Python a dict.
levels.expert: The load factor α = n / m, entries per bucket, sets the speed: with chaining, a successful search checks about 1 + α/2 entries on average under uniform hashing. Maps grow, often doubling, when α passes a threshold, so one insert can cost O(n) while the amortized cost stays O(1). A bad or attacker-chosen hash piles keys into one bucket and drags lookups toward O(n), which is why runtimes randomize their hash seeds.

cards.analogy: A hash map is like a coat check: you hand over your coat and get a numbered ticket, and the ticket takes the attendant straight to the right hook instead of searching every coat.

formula.name: Load factor
formula.expression: α = n / m
formula.spoken: the load factor alpha equals the number of entries n divided by the number of buckets m
formula.assumptions: Keys spread evenly over the buckets, called uniform hashing.

example.explain: Counting words with a Map: "buy" appears 2 times, "the" 3 times, a missing word counts 0, and there are 6 different words.

quiz.q: What is the average time to look up a key in a hash map?
quiz.a: O(1), constant time on average.

quiz.q: What is a collision?
quiz.a: Two different keys landing in the same bucket; the map keeps both and compares the keys.

quiz.q: A map holds 600 entries in 800 buckets. What is its load factor?
quiz.a: 0.75, which is 600 divided by 800.

misconceptions: O(1) on average is not a promise for every single operation: a resize or a crowded bucket can be slow.

cards.title: Sorting and merge sort
cards.summary: Merge sort splits a list in halves, sorts them and merges them back in order.

levels.beginner: Sorting puts items in order, smallest to largest or A to Z. Merge sort does it by splitting the list in half again and again until every piece has one item, then merging the pieces back together in order, like combining two sorted piles of cards.
levels.intermediate: Merging two sorted lists takes at most one comparison per item placed, and a list can be halved about log₂ n times, so merge sort makes about n·log₂ n comparisons: O(n log n) in every case, against O(n²) for simple methods like insertion sort. It is stable, keeping equal items in their original order, and it needs extra memory for the merge.
levels.expert: Merge sort's cost follows T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, which solves to Θ(n log n); its comparisons never exceed n⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2^⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1, which is below n⌈log₂ n⌉. No comparison sort can beat about n log₂ n in the worst case, because it must tell apart n! possible orders and log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n. Real libraries use hybrids such as Timsort, which finds runs that are already sorted and uses insertion sort for small pieces.

cards.analogy: Merge sort is like two people each sorting half a deck of cards, then laying the two sorted piles side by side and always taking the smaller top card.

formula.name: Merge sort comparisons, worst case
formula.expression: comparisons(n) ≤ n⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2^⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1
formula.spoken: merge sort makes at most n times the ceiling of log base 2 of n, minus 2 to the power of that ceiling, plus 1, comparisons
formula.assumptions: Top-down merge sort that compares two items at a time.

example.explain: Merge sort puts 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4 in order with 17 comparisons, exactly the worst case for 8 items: 8 times 3, minus 8, plus 1.

quiz.q: What is merge sort's running time?
quiz.a: O(n log n), in the best, average and worst case.

quiz.q: What does a stable sort keep?
quiz.a: Equal items in their original order.

quiz.q: At most how many comparisons does merge sort need for 8 items?
quiz.a: 17, from 8 times 3, minus 8, plus 1.

misconceptions: O(n log n) does not mean merge sort is always fastest: for small or nearly sorted lists insertion sort can win.

cards.title: HTTP and APIs
cards.summary: An API is the menu one program offers another; on the web its requests travel over HTTP.

levels.beginner: An API is a menu one program offers another: the requests it accepts and what it sends back. On the web those requests travel over HTTP: an app asks a server for something at an address, and the server answers with a status code and some data.
levels.intermediate: An HTTP request has a method (GET reads, POST creates or sends, PUT and PATCH change, DELETE removes), a URL with an optional query string, headers such as Content-Type and Authorization, and sometimes a JSON body. The status code's first digit says what happened: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the caller's mistake, 5xx the server's failure.
levels.expert: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, meaning that repeating them leaves the same result, so they can be retried safely; POST is not, unless the API takes an idempotency key. Retry 429 and 5xx answers with exponential backoff and jitter, never other 4xx ones, and put a timeout on every call. Credentials never belong in a URL, where they end up in logs: they go in a header, over HTTPS.

cards.analogy: An API is like a restaurant menu and waiter: you order from the menu in a set way, the kitchen does work you can't see, and the waiter brings back your dish or tells you it's sold out.

example.explain: It builds the address https://api.example.com/v1/bars?symbol=MNQ&interval=5m and sorts status codes into their classes: 200 is success, 404 a client error and 503 a server error.

quiz.q: Which status code class means the caller made a mistake?
quiz.a: 4xx, such as 404 Not Found or 401 Unauthorized.

quiz.q: Which methods are idempotent?
quiz.a: GET, PUT and DELETE: repeating them gives the same result.

quiz.q: Should a 400 Bad Request be retried?
quiz.a: No. Fix the request. Retry only 429 and 5xx answers, with backoff.

misconceptions: A 200 status does not always mean the work succeeded: some APIs return 200 with an error inside the body, so check the body too.

cards.title: Concurrency and async
cards.summary: Concurrency keeps several jobs in progress at once, so waiting does not waste time.

levels.beginner: Concurrency means juggling several jobs at once instead of finishing one before starting the next. While one job waits, for example for a website to answer, the program gets on with another, so the waiting doesn't waste time.
levels.intermediate: In JavaScript, slow work returns a Promise, a placeholder for a result that arrives later, and await pauses only that one function until it settles. Promise.all starts several waits together and finishes when all are done, so three one-second requests take about one second instead of three. It fails as soon as any one fails; Promise.allSettled reports every result instead.
levels.expert: Concurrency is about structure, many tasks in progress; parallelism is about execution, many at the same instant on several cores. Shared changing state invites race conditions, so prefer messages, unchanging data or one owner per piece of state, which is what a Durable Object gives CHE's Worker. Amdahl's law caps the speed-up: if a share p of the work can run in parallel on N workers, the speed-up is 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N), never more than 1 / (1 − p).

cards.analogy: Concurrency is like a cook with three pans on the stove: while the pasta boils, the sauce gets stirred, instead of watching one pot until it is done.

formula.name: Amdahl's law
formula.spoken: the speed-up on N workers equals 1 divided by the serial share, 1 minus p, plus the parallel share p divided by N

variables.meaning: the share of the work that can run in parallel
the speed-up compared with one worker

formula.assumptions: The parallel part splits perfectly and the problem size stays fixed.

example.explain: Three timed tasks run together under Promise.all: all 3 are in flight at once, they finish fastest first, and the results still come back in the order they were asked for.

quiz.q: What does await do?
quiz.a: It pauses only that async function until the Promise settles; the rest of the program keeps running.

quiz.q: Three one-second requests run with Promise.all. About how long does it take?
quiz.a: About one second, because they wait at the same time.

quiz.q: With 90% parallel work on 4 cores, what speed-up does Amdahl's law give?
quiz.a: About 3.08 times: 1 divided by 0.1 plus 0.9 over 4.

misconceptions: async does not make code run in parallel on its own: JavaScript still runs one piece of code at a time, it just stops waiting idly.

cards.title: Ticks, points and contract value
cards.summary: Futures prices move in ticks, and each contract sets how many dollars a point is worth.

levels.beginner: Futures prices move in fixed steps called ticks. Each contract also has a point value: how many dollars one full point of price movement is worth. On MNQ, the Micro Nasdaq-100 future, a point is $2 and the smallest step, a tick, is a quarter point, so one tick is $0.50.
levels.intermediate: Profit or loss is points moved × point value × contracts, before costs. NQ and MNQ follow the same index, but an NQ point is worth $20 and an MNQ point $2, so one NQ is the exposure of ten MNQ. A 10-point move on 2 MNQ is 10 × $2 × 2 = $40; the same move on 1 NQ is $200.
levels.expert: The multiplier sets the notional exposure, index level × point value: at 21,000 one MNQ controls about $42,000 and one NQ about $420,000, which is why a small margin deposit carries large leverage. Ticks make stops discrete: a stop 10 points away is 40 ticks. Commissions are fixed per contract while a point's value scales with the multiplier, so on micros the costs are a larger share of each point.

cards.analogy: Point value is like the price per gallon at a pump: the display moves the same way for everyone, but how many dollars each step costs you depends on the size of your tank, the contract.

formula.name: Futures profit and loss
formula.expression: P&L = points × point value × contracts;  tick value = tick size × point value
formula.spoken: profit or loss equals points moved times point value times contracts, and tick value equals tick size times point value

variables.meaning: price moved, exit minus entry for a long

formula.assumptions: Before commissions, fees, spread and slippage.

steps: 10 points × $2 per point × 2 MNQ contracts = $40, before costs
An MNQ tick is 0.25 × $2 = $0.50; an NQ tick is 0.25 × $20 = $5.00

quiz.q: How many dollars is one MNQ tick?
quiz.a: $0.50: a quarter point times $2.

quiz.q: What is a 5-point move on 3 MNQ worth, before costs?
How many MNQ contracts match one NQ in exposure?
quiz.a: Ten, because $20 ÷ $2 = 10.

misconceptions: A micro is not a smaller-risk version of the same trade by magic: ten micros carry exactly the risk of one full contract.
limitations: Specs are CME's and can change: verify against the exchange.
Profit and loss here is before commissions, fees, spread and slippage.

cards.title: Bid, ask and spread
cards.summary: The bid is the best price to sell at now, the ask the best price to buy at; the gap is the spread.

levels.beginner: Every market shows two prices at once. The bid is the highest price a buyer is offering right now; the ask, or offer, is the lowest price a seller will take. The gap between them is the spread. Buy at market and you pay the ask; sell at market and you get the bid, so crossing the spread is a cost you pay straight away.
levels.intermediate: Spread = ask − bid, often counted in ticks. On MNQ a tick is 0.25 points, worth $0.50 a contract, so a one-tick spread costs $0.50 a contract to cross, and a round trip with market orders pays it going in and coming out, about half on each side. A limit order can wait at the bid or ask to avoid paying the spread, but it might not fill.
levels.expert: The quoted spread is only the visible cost. The effective spread, 2 × |fill price − midpoint|, measures what fills really paid, and slippage adds the price moving between the decision and the fill. Spreads widen when liquidity is thin: around economic releases, near the open and overnight. A strategy whose average edge per trade is close to its round-trip costs has no real edge, which is why CHE's paper engine charges spread and slippage on every simulated trade.

cards.analogy: The spread is like a currency booth at the airport: it buys your dollars at one price and sells them at a higher one, and the difference is its fee for being there when you need it.

formula.name: Spread and its cost
formula.expression: spread = ask − bid;  cost = (spread ÷ tick size) × tick value × contracts
formula.spoken: the spread equals the ask minus the bid, and its cost equals the spread in ticks times the tick value times the contracts

variables.meaning: the best offer to sell to you and the best bid to buy from you

cards.title: R-multiples
cards.summary: R is what you planned to risk on a trade; results in R compare trades of any size.

levels.beginner: R is the amount you planned to risk on a trade: the distance from your entry to your stop. Measuring results in R makes trades comparable: winning twice what you risked is +2R, and getting stopped out is −1R, whatever the contract or size.
levels.intermediate: For a long, R-multiple = (exit − entry) ÷ (entry − stop); for a short, (entry − exit) ÷ (stop − entry). The planned reward-to-risk is the same sum with the target in place of the exit. Bought at 100 with a stop at 98 and sold at 105, the trade made 5 points on 2 points of risk: +2.5R. CHE's paper engine records both r_gross, before costs, and r_net, after them.
levels.expert: A strategy's list of R-multiples is the raw material for its statistics: their mean is the expectancy and their spread sets how deep losing streaks go. The initial risk must be fixed at entry; moving the stop later changes what the trade really risked, and slippage through a stop can make a loss worse than −1R. R removes position size, so different sizes compare fairly, but it also hides how many dollars were at stake.

cards.analogy: R is like measuring a trip in tanks of fuel instead of miles: three tanks means the same thing whether you drive a small car or a truck.

formula.name: R-multiple of a long trade
formula.expression: R = (exit − entry) ÷ (entry − stop)
formula.spoken: R equals the exit minus the entry, divided by the entry minus the stop

variables.meaning: the initial stop, below the entry for a long

formula.assumptions: A long trade with the initial stop fixed at entry; before costs unless the exit includes them. For a short, R = (entry − exit) ÷ (stop − entry).

quiz.q: A long enters at 50 with a stop at 48 and exits at 54. What is its R-multiple?
quiz.a: +2R: 4 points gained on 2 points risked.

quiz.q: A trade stopped out exactly at its stop is worth how many R?
quiz.a: −1R, before costs.

quiz.q: Why measure trades in R?
quiz.a: It makes results comparable across contracts and position sizes.

misconceptions: A high reward-to-risk plan is not better by itself: a 5R target that is rarely reached can have a worse expectancy than a 1R target.
limitations: R hides position size: two trades of +1R can be very different amounts of money.
Slippage through a stop can make a loss worse than −1R.

cards.title: Risk management and position sizing
cards.summary: Decide the loss you can take before entering, and size the position from it.

levels.beginner: Risk management means deciding, before you enter, how much you can lose on a trade, and placing a stop where you will get out if you are wrong. A common rule is to risk only a small fixed slice of the account, often 1% or less, so a run of losses hurts but does not end the account.
levels.intermediate: The position size comes from the risk, not the other way round: contracts = risk budget ÷ (stop distance in points × point value), rounded down. With $100 to risk and a 10-point stop on MNQ at $2 a point, each contract risks $20, so the size is 5 contracts. If even one contract would risk more than the budget, the trade is skipped.
levels.expert: Fixed-fraction sizing shrinks positions after losses and grows them after wins, which slows the damage of a drawdown. Losing streaks are normal: at a 40% win rate the chance that any given 10 trades all lose is 0.6¹⁰, about 0.6%, yet over hundreds of trades a streak like that becomes likely. Correlated positions, gaps through stops and leverage all make the real risk bigger than the plan, so a daily loss limit and a maximum size per order are a second line of defence.

cards.analogy: Position sizing is like deciding how much water to pour into each bucket before carrying them over a rickety bridge: if one bucket falls, you lose only what was in it.

formula.name: Position size
formula.expression: contracts = floor(risk budget ÷ (stop distance × point value))
formula.spoken: contracts equal the risk budget divided by the stop distance times the point value, rounded down

variables.meaning: the most you accept losing on this trade

formula.assumptions: The stop fills at its price; gaps and slippage can make the real loss bigger. Costs come on top.

quiz.q: You risk $60 with a 15-point stop on MNQ. How many contracts?
quiz.a: 2: each contract risks 15 × $2 = $30, and $60 ÷ $30 = 2.

quiz.q: Which comes first, the position size or the stop?
quiz.a: The stop, where the idea is proven wrong; the size follows from it.

quiz.q: What does a 1% risk rule mean on a $10,000 account?
quiz.a: Risk at most $100 on one trade.

misconceptions: A tight stop is not automatically lower risk: it can mean a bigger size, more stop-outs and more slippage.
limitations: The stop is assumed to fill at its price; gaps and fast markets fill worse.
Position size from one trade's stop ignores correlated positions held at the same time.

cards.title: Expectancy
cards.summary: What a strategy makes or loses on an average trade, over many trades.

levels.beginner: Expectancy is what a strategy makes or loses on an average trade, over many trades. A strategy can lose more often than it wins and still have a positive expectancy if its wins are big enough, and one that wins often can still lose money if its losses are bigger.
levels.intermediate: In R: expectancy = win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss, which is the same as the mean of all the trades' R-multiples. Winning 40% of the time at +2R and losing 60% at −1R gives 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = +0.2R a trade: risking $50 a trade, about $10 a trade on average over the long run, before costs.
levels.expert: Expectancy is an estimate with uncertainty: its 95% range is roughly the mean ± 1.96 × s ÷ √n, so a positive mean whose range includes zero is not yet evidence of an edge. Measure it after costs and slippage, out of sample, on trades taken by fixed rules; tuning rules on the same data that measures them inflates it. CHE's promotion test asks for a 95% range above zero, at least 30 out-of-sample trades and profitable walk-forward folds.

cards.analogy: Expectancy is like a shop's average profit per customer: some buy nothing and some buy a lot, but the average over many days decides whether the shop survives.

formula.name: Expectancy in R
formula.spoken: expectancy equals the win rate times the average win, minus the loss rate times the average loss, all in R

variables.meaning: average losing trade, as a positive number

formula.assumptions: No breakeven trades (otherwise use the mean of all R-multiples); measured after costs on many out-of-sample trades taken by fixed rules.

quiz.q: Win rate 50%, average win 1.5R, average loss 1R. What is the expectancy?
Can a strategy that wins only 30% of the time have a positive expectancy?
quiz.a: Yes, if its average win is more than about 2.33 times its average loss.

quiz.q: Why isn't a positive average over 12 trades proof of an edge?
quiz.a: The sample is too small: the 95% range of the mean is wide and usually includes zero.

misconceptions: A high win rate is not a positive expectancy: what matters is win rate and payoff together.
limitations: An estimate from past trades: its range must be read with it, and the future can differ.
Measured after assumed costs; real fills can be worse.

cards.title: Win rate and its confidence interval
cards.summary: The share of winning trades, always read with its honest range.

levels.beginner: Win rate is the share of trades that made money: 12 winners out of 20 trades is 60%. On its own it says little: a 90% win rate loses money if the rare losses are huge, and with only a few trades the rate is mostly luck.
levels.intermediate: Report a win rate with its range. The Wilson 95% interval for w wins in n trades stays honest even with few trades: 12 wins in 20 gives about 38.7% to 78.1%, so the true rate could easily be under 50%. The range narrows with 1 ÷ √n, so four times the trades halves its width.
levels.expert: Wilson's centre is (p̂ + z²/2n) ÷ (1 + z²/n) and its half-width z·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n + z²/4n²) ÷ (1 + z²/n), with z = 1.96 for 95%. Unlike the simple p̂ ± z·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n), it never goes below 0 or above 100% and still works at 0 or n wins. It assumes independent trades with one fixed win probability, which regime changes and clustered trades break, and a win rate must always be read with the payoff, which is why CHE never reports it alone.

cards.analogy: A win rate from a few trades is like judging a basketball player on five free throws: they might hit four by luck, so you give a range, not a single number, until you've seen a few hundred.

formula.name: Wilson 95% interval
formula.expression: centre = (p̂ + z²/2n) ÷ (1 + z²/n);  half-width = z·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n + z²/4n²) ÷ (1 + z²/n);  p̂ = w ÷ n
formula.spoken: the Wilson interval is a centre plus or minus a half-width: the centre is the win rate plus z squared over 2 n, divided by 1 plus z squared over n, and the half-width is z times the square root of the win rate times the loss rate over n, plus z squared over 4 n squared, divided by the same 1 plus z squared over n
formula.assumptions: Independent trades with one fixed win probability; z = 1.96 for 95%.

quiz.q: You won 6 of your last 10 trades. Is your win rate 60%?
quiz.a: Measured, yes, but the 95% range is about 31% to 83%, so the true rate is very uncertain.

quiz.q: Why can a 90% win rate still lose money?
quiz.a: If the average loss is more than nine times the average win, the losses outweigh the wins.

quiz.q: How many more trades roughly halve the width of the range?
quiz.a: About four times as many, because the width shrinks with 1 ÷ √n.

misconceptions: A 60% win rate from 10 trades is not "a 60% strategy": the honest range runs from about 31% to 83%.
limitations: Assumes independent trades with one fixed win probability, which regime changes break.
A win rate means nothing without the payoff.

cards.title: Profit factor
cards.summary: Dollars won for every dollar lost: gross profit divided by gross loss.

levels.beginner: Profit factor is how many dollars a strategy made for every dollar it lost: all the winning trades added up, divided by all the losing trades added up. Above 1 it made money overall, below 1 it lost, and exactly 1 broke even.
levels.intermediate: Profit factor = gross profit ÷ gross loss, with the loss counted as a positive number, after costs: $600 won and $400 lost gives 1.5. It folds win rate and payoff into one number, but it ignores the order of trades, so two strategies with the same profit factor can have very different drawdowns. With no losing trades it is undefined, not infinite proof of skill.
levels.expert: Profit factor ties to the payoff: with win rate p and payoff ratio b, average win ÷ average loss, PF = p·b ÷ (1 − p) when there are no breakeven trades. A few outliers move it a lot, so one huge win can carry a weak strategy; check it with the largest trade removed and fold by fold in a walk-forward test. CHE's promotion test asks for a profit factor above 1.2 after costs, out of sample, together with a positive expectancy range.

cards.analogy: Profit factor is like a farmer comparing what the harvest sold for with what the seed and fuel cost: above 1 the season paid, below 1 it cost him.

formula.name: Profit factor
formula.expression: PF = gross profit ÷ gross loss
formula.spoken: profit factor equals gross profit divided by gross loss

variables.meaning: the winning trades added up, after costs
the losing trades added up, as a positive number

formula.assumptions: After costs; undefined when no trade lost.

What does a profit factor of 0.8 mean?
quiz.a: The strategy lost money: 80 cents won for every dollar lost.

quiz.q: Win rate 50% and an average win twice the average loss: what is the profit factor?

misconceptions: A profit factor above 1 in a backtest is not an edge until it holds out of sample and after costs.
limitations: Ignores the order of trades, so it says nothing about drawdowns.
A few large trades can move it a lot.

cards.title: Maximum drawdown
cards.summary: How far the account fell from its highest point; the maximum is the worst such fall.

levels.beginner: Drawdown is how far your account has fallen from its highest point. If it grew to $11,000 and then dropped to $9,900, the drawdown is $1,100, or 10%. The maximum drawdown is the deepest fall over the whole history: the worst stretch you would have had to sit through.
levels.intermediate: Follow the equity trade by trade, keep the highest value so far, the peak, and the drawdown at each point is peak − equity; the maximum drawdown is the largest of those. Profits of +100, −50, −80, +200 and −30 give equity of 100, 50, −30, 170 and 140, and a maximum drawdown of 130, from the peak of 100 down to −30. Recovery is harder than the fall: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back.
levels.expert: Maximum drawdown depends on the order of trades, so one backtest shows only one path; reshuffling the same trades, a Monte Carlo of the sequence, shows how deep it could plausibly have been. Drawdowns get deeper with more trades and more volatility, so the worst is usually still ahead of a short record. After a fractional drawdown d, recovery needs a gain of d ÷ (1 − d). Ratios such as Calmar, return ÷ maximum drawdown, compare strategies on this pain.

cards.analogy: Drawdown is like a hiker's drop from the highest point reached so far: the summit only counts until the trail goes down, and what matters is how deep the valley gets before the next climb.

formula.name: Maximum drawdown
formula.expression: MDD = max over t of (highest equity up to t − equity at t)
formula.spoken: maximum drawdown is the largest gap between the highest equity reached so far and the equity at any later point

variables.meaning: closed-trade equity after trade t, starting from zero

formula.assumptions: Closed trades in time order, starting from zero; swings while a trade is open can make the real drawdown deeper.

quiz.q: An account falls from $20,000 to $15,000. What is the drawdown in percent?
After a 25% drawdown, what gain gets back to the peak?
Why can the next drawdown be deeper than the backtest's?
quiz.a: The backtest shows one order of trades; other orders and a longer history can go deeper.

misconceptions: A backtest's maximum drawdown is not the worst you will see: it is the worst of one path.
limitations: One path only: other orders of the same trades can go deeper.
Closed-trade equity misses the swings while trades are open.

cards.title: VWAP
cards.summary: The session's average traded price, weighted by volume.

levels.beginner: VWAP, the volume-weighted average price, is the average price traded so far in the session, where prices that traded more volume count more. Traders use it as a fair-value line: price above VWAP means buyers have paid up on average, below it means sellers have pushed it down.
levels.intermediate: VWAP = Σ(typical price × volume) ÷ Σ volume, added up bar by bar from the session start, with typical price = (high + low + close) ÷ 3 on bar data. It starts again each session, so it is an intraday tool. Big traders judge their own fills against it: buying below VWAP counts as a good execution.
levels.expert: On bars the typical price is an approximation; the true VWAP adds up every trade's price × size. The session start decides the value, so a futures VWAP from the 6 p.m. open differs from one anchored at the 9:30 New York open, and an anchored VWAP starts from a chosen event instead. Deviation bands use the volume-weighted standard deviation of price around VWAP. VWAP describes, it does not predict: price crossing it is not an edge without tested evidence.

cards.analogy: VWAP is like the average price per gallon a gas station sold at today, where a truck filling 100 gallons counts for more than a scooter filling one.

formula.name: VWAP
formula.expression: VWAP = Σ(TPᵢ × Vᵢ) ÷ ΣVᵢ,  TP = (H + L + C) ÷ 3
formula.spoken: VWAP equals the sum of typical price times volume, divided by the sum of volume, where typical price is high plus low plus close, divided by 3

variables.meaning: the bar's high, low and close

formula.assumptions: Summed from the session start; the bar typical price approximates the true trade-by-trade VWAP.

quiz.q: Two trades: 100 contracts at 10 and 300 at 12. What is the VWAP?
Does VWAP carry over from yesterday?
quiz.a: No. It starts again at each session, unless you anchor it somewhere else on purpose.

quiz.q: Is a close above VWAP a buy signal?
quiz.a: Not by itself. VWAP describes the session; only tested evidence turns a rule into an edge.

misconceptions: VWAP is not a support line that price must respect: it is an average of what already traded.
limitations: Bar typical prices approximate trade prices; delayed public bars may have partial volume.
VWAP describes the session; it does not predict.

cards.title: Sample size and out-of-sample testing
cards.summary: A few trades can look great by luck; only many trades, on untouched data, are evidence.

levels.beginner: A handful of trades can look great by pure luck, the way a coin can land heads five times in a row. Results start to mean something only after many trades, and only on data the strategy was not tuned on. CHE treats fewer than 30 trades as anecdote, not evidence.
levels.intermediate: The uncertainty of an average shrinks with the square root of the sample: the standard error of the mean R is s ÷ √n, and the 95% range is the mean ± 1.96 × s ÷ √n. A mean of 0.2R with a spread of 1.2R over 36 trades has a standard error of 0.2R, so the range is about −0.19R to +0.59R: it includes zero, so no edge is shown yet. Walk-forward testing tunes nothing on the test period: the rules are frozen, then measured on later data, fold by fold.
levels.expert: Testing many variants and keeping the best is selection bias: the winner's backtest overstates its future, the more so the more variants were tried, so the bar for evidence must rise with the number tested. Look-ahead (using data not yet known at the time), survivorship (only instruments that still exist) and leaving out costs all inflate results. CHE's evidence engine computes indicators from past bars only, journals losing trades and failed experiments, and promotes nothing without 30 or more out-of-sample trades, an expectancy range above zero, a profit factor above 1.2 and mostly profitable walk-forward folds.

cards.analogy: A small sample is like judging a restaurant on one meal: maybe the chef had a great night. You trust the rating only after many meals, ideally ones the restaurant didn't know you were judging.

formula.name: 95% range of the mean R
formula.expression: mean ± 1.96 × s ÷ √n
formula.spoken: the 95 percent range is the mean plus or minus 1.96 times the standard deviation divided by the square root of n
formula.assumptions: Independent trades; the normal approximation is rough below about 30 trades.

quiz.q: Mean 0.3R, standard deviation 1.5R, 100 trades: what is the 95% range?
quiz.a: About +0.006R to +0.594R: 0.3 ± 1.96 × 0.15, just above zero.

quiz.q: How many trades does it take to halve the standard error?
quiz.a: Four times as many, because it shrinks with √n.

quiz.q: You tested 50 variants and kept the best. Why is its backtest too optimistic?
quiz.a: Selection bias: the best of many is partly the luckiest, so its future is likely worse.

misconceptions: More backtest variants do not make the best one more trustworthy: they make it more likely to be luck.
limitations: The normal approximation is rough below about 30 trades.
Correlated trades carry less information than their count suggests.

cards.title: Order types and bracket orders
cards.summary: Market, limit, stop and stop-limit orders, and brackets that attach a stop and a target.

levels.beginner: A market order fills now at the best price available. A limit order fills only at your price or better, so it may not fill. A stop order waits until price reaches a level, then becomes a market order; it is how a stop-loss gets you out. A bracket sends an entry with a stop and a target attached.
levels.intermediate: A stop-limit becomes a limit order when its stop price trades, so it controls the fill price but can be skipped entirely in a fast move, which is dangerous for a protective stop. In a bracket the stop and the target are one-cancels-other (OCO): when one fills, the other is cancelled. The plan's reward-to-risk is the target distance divided by the stop distance.
levels.expert: Market and stop orders pay the spread and slippage; limit orders earn the spread but face adverse selection, filling most often when price is about to go through them. Exchanges protect market orders with price bands, and brokers may simulate stop or OCO orders on their own servers, so the order type you choose and where it lives change what happens in a gap or an outage. Test the fill model you assume.

cards.analogy: A limit order is like a standing offer on a house at your price: you may get it, or the house sells to someone else. A market order is like paying the asking price today.

formula.name: Reward-to-risk of a bracket
formula.expression: reward ÷ risk = |target − entry| ÷ |entry − stop|;  break-even win rate = risk ÷ (risk + reward)
formula.spoken: reward to risk equals the target distance divided by the stop distance, and the break-even win rate equals the risk divided by risk plus reward
formula.assumptions: Fills exactly at entry, stop and target; the trade ends at one of them. Costs and slippage raise the break-even win rate.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
win rate needed to break even before costs = 10 ÷ (10 + 30) = 25.0%

quiz.q: A short enters at 100 with a stop at 102 and a target at 94. What is the reward to risk?
quiz.a: 3 to 1: 6 points of reward on 2 points of risk.

quiz.q: Which order can be skipped entirely in a fast market, a stop or a stop-limit?
quiz.a: A stop-limit: once triggered it is a limit order and may not fill.

quiz.q: In a bracket, what happens to the target when the stop fills?
quiz.a: It is cancelled: the stop and target are one-cancels-other.

misconceptions: A stop order does not guarantee its price: once triggered it fills at the market, which can be worse.
limitations: Order behaviour differs by exchange and broker, especially for simulated stops and OCO links; read the broker's rules.
A 3-to-1 plan says nothing about how often the target is reached.

cards.title: Order book, liquidity and slippage
cards.summary: The book lists resting orders at each price; a large market order eats through it and pays slippage.

levels.beginner: The order book is the list of limit orders waiting to buy and sell at each price. Liquidity is how much is waiting near the current price. When you buy with a market order you take the cheapest offers first; if your order is bigger than the first level, the rest fills at worse prices. The difference is slippage.
levels.intermediate: A market buy fills level by level: the average fill is the total paid divided by the quantity. Slippage is the average fill minus the best ask, times the point value and the quantity. A thin book, an economic release or the overnight session make each level smaller, so the same order slips more. Limit orders add liquidity; market orders remove it.
levels.expert: Visible depth is not the whole book: iceberg orders hide size, and quotes are pulled in milliseconds when price moves, so depth often vanishes exactly when it is needed. Price impact grows with order size relative to the volume traded, roughly with its square root in many studies. A backtest that fills every order at the last price ignores all of this, which flatters fast, small-target strategies the most.

cards.analogy: Buying through the book is like buying apples from a row of stalls: the first stall is cheapest, but if you want more than it has you walk to the next, dearer one.

formula.name: Market order through the book
formula.expression: average fill = Σ(price × size taken) ÷ quantity;  slippage = (average fill − best price) × point value × quantity
formula.spoken: the average fill is the total paid divided by the quantity, and slippage is the average fill minus the best price, times the point value and the quantity

variables.meaning: each level of the book on the side being hit

formula.assumptions: The book stays still while the order fills; in practice it moves and hidden orders change the result.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
slippage = 0.225 points × $2.00 × 10 = $4.50 against the best price 21,000.25

quiz.q: You buy 10 MNQ: 4 fill at 21,000.25, 3 at 21,000.50, 3 at 21,000.75. What is the average fill?
Why does slippage grow around economic releases?
quiz.a: Resting orders are pulled, so each price level holds less and an order reaches deeper prices.

quiz.q: Does a limit order pay the spread?
quiz.a: No, it waits to be filled at its price, but it may not fill.

misconceptions: The best bid and ask are not the price for any size: only for the size shown at that level.
limitations: Real books change while an order fills, and hidden orders are not shown; the result is a model.
CHE has no order-book data, so it cannot measure real slippage for the owner's orders.

cards.title: Stocks and share sizing
cards.summary: A share is a small piece of a company; size a stock trade by the dollars between entry and stop.

levels.beginner: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company, and its price moves with what buyers and sellers will pay. A stock trade is sized the same way as a futures trade: decide the most you will lose, place the stop where the idea is wrong, and buy only as many shares as that loss allows.
levels.intermediate: Shares = risk budget ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down. Risking $100 with an entry at $50 and a stop at $48 risks $2 a share, so the size is 50 shares, which costs $2,500 to buy: the capital is not the risk. The R-multiple of the result is the gain per share divided by the $2 risked.
levels.expert: Stocks gap: news outside trading hours can open the price far beyond the stop, so the planned loss is a minimum, not a maximum. Liquidity varies hugely between large and small companies, and short selling adds borrow costs and the risk of a squeeze. Splits and dividends change historical prices, so a backtest needs adjusted data and must include the companies that were delisted, or it suffers survivorship bias.

cards.analogy: Sizing a stock trade is like deciding how many tiles to buy from the size of the room, not from how much money is in your pocket.

formula.name: Shares from risk
formula.expression: shares = floor(risk budget ÷ |entry − stop|)
formula.spoken: shares equal the risk budget divided by the distance from entry to stop, rounded down

variables.meaning: the planned entry and stop prices

formula.assumptions: The stop fills at its price; an overnight gap can open far beyond it. Commissions are not included.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
capital to buy them = 50 × $50.00 = $2,500.00; the risk is $100.00, not the whole amount

quiz.q: You risk $75 with an entry at $20.00 and a stop at $19.50. How many shares?
Is the money needed to buy the shares the same as the risk?
quiz.a: No: the risk is shares × the stop distance; the capital is shares × the price.

quiz.q: Why is a stock's planned loss a minimum, not a maximum?
quiz.a: Because the price can gap past the stop overnight or on news.

misconceptions: Buying fewer, more expensive shares is not safer by itself: the risk depends on the stop distance times the shares.
limitations: Gaps, halts and thin trading can make the real loss far bigger than the plan.
Commissions, borrow fees for shorts and taxes are not included.

cards.title: Options basics at expiry
cards.summary: Calls and puts: the right to buy or sell at a strike, with a breakeven and a known worst case for the buyer.

levels.beginner: An option is a contract that gives its buyer the right, not the duty, to buy (a call) or sell (a put) a stock at a set price, the strike, until a date. The buyer pays a premium for that right, and that premium is the most the buyer can lose. A standard stock option covers 100 shares.
levels.intermediate: At expiry a call is worth max(0, stock − strike) and a put max(0, strike − stock): that is intrinsic value. The buyer of a call breaks even at strike + premium; the buyer of a put at strike − premium. A long call with a $100 strike bought for $3 risks $300 and is worth $1,000 at a stock price of $110, a $700 profit.
levels.expert: Before expiry an option also carries time value, which depends on volatility, time left and interest rates, and needs a pricing model such as Black-Scholes and live quotes, which CHE does not have. Sellers collect the premium but take the other side: a short call has unlimited risk, and a short put can lose almost the whole strike. American options can be exercised early, and assignment can arrive without warning.

cards.analogy: A call option is like a deposit on a house at a fixed price: if prices rise you buy cheap, and if they fall you walk away and lose only the deposit.

formula.name: Option payoff at expiry
formula.expression: call: intrinsic = max(0, S − K), breakeven = K + premium;  put: intrinsic = max(0, K − S), breakeven = K − premium;  P&L = (intrinsic − premium) × 100 × contracts
formula.spoken: a call is worth the stock minus the strike, or zero, and breaks even at the strike plus the premium; a put is worth the strike minus the stock, or zero, and breaks even at the strike minus the premium
formula.assumptions: At expiry only, held to expiry, no early exercise, before commissions.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
most it can gain = unlimited, because the price can keep rising

quiz.q: A put with a $50 strike costs $2. Where does the buyer break even at expiry?
quiz.a: $48: the strike minus the premium.

quiz.q: What is the most the buyer of a $3 call can lose on one contract?
quiz.a: $300: the premium times 100 shares.

quiz.q: What is the risk of selling a call without owning the stock?
quiz.a: Unlimited, because the stock can keep rising.

misconceptions: An option that expires below its breakeven is not always a total loss: between the strike and the breakeven some premium is recovered.
limitations: Payoffs at expiry only; before expiry the price depends on volatility and time, which needs a model and live quotes CHE does not have.

cards.title: Price action, candles and volume
cards.summary: Reading bars directly: the body, the wicks, the range, and volume compared with recent bars.

levels.beginner: Price action means reading what price did, bar by bar, instead of an indicator. Each candle has an open, a high, a low and a close. The body runs from open to close; the thin wicks show where price went and was pushed back. Volume is how much traded in the bar.
levels.intermediate: Body = |close − open|; upper wick = high − the higher of open and close; lower wick = the lower of open and close − low. A body that fills most of the range shows one side in control; long wicks show rejection. Relative volume, this bar's volume divided by the average of recent bars, says whether the move had unusual participation.
levels.expert: Candle patterns have weak and unstable evidence once costs are counted: studies such as Lo, Mamaysky and Wang find some patterns carry a little information, but far less than chart books suggest, and results depend on the bar size. Futures volume from a delayed public feed may be partial. Treat price action as a description that a rule must turn into a tested hypothesis.

cards.analogy: A candle is like a day's weather summary: where the temperature started, how hot and cold it got, and where it ended up.

formula.name: Candle anatomy and relative volume
formula.expression: body = |C − O|;  upper wick = H − max(O, C);  lower wick = min(O, C) − L;  relative volume = V ÷ average prior V
formula.spoken: the body is the close minus the open, the wicks are what lies beyond the body, and relative volume is the volume divided by the average of the bars before

variables.meaning: the bar's open, high, low and close

formula.assumptions: One bar of one time frame; a different bar size shows the same move differently.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
relative volume = 3,000 ÷ average 1,500 of the 4 bars before = 2

quiz.q: A bar opens at 50, trades from 49 to 55 and closes at 54. How long is its upper wick?
A bar trades 6,000 contracts when the last bars averaged 2,000. What is its relative volume?
Is a hammer candle a buy signal on its own?
quiz.a: No. Without a tested rule and costs it is only a description.

misconceptions: High volume does not tell you who won: every contract bought was also sold.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.
Delayed public futures volume may not match the exchange total.

cards.title: Market structure: BOS and CHOCH
cards.summary: Swing highs and lows define a trend; a break of structure continues it, a change of character flips it.

levels.beginner: Market structure is the pattern of swing highs and swing lows. Higher highs and higher lows make an uptrend; lower highs and lower lows a downtrend. A break of structure (BOS) is price closing past the last swing in the trend's direction. A change of character (CHOCH) is the first close past a swing against the trend.
levels.intermediate: The difference is direction against the trend: in an uptrend, a close above the last swing high is a BOS, the trend going on; the first close below the last swing low is a CHOCH, the first sign it may be turning. A swing is only known after the bars beside it close, so every label must wait for that confirmation.
levels.expert: Labels depend on choices: how many bars make a swing, whether a wick or only a close counts, and which time frame rules. With a swing size of 1 or 2, noise produces many breaks; with larger sizes, the label arrives late. Defined this way it is a mechanical rule that can be backtested causally, which is the only way to learn whether it adds anything after costs; CHE's sweep-then-structure-shift strategy is one such test.

cards.analogy: Structure is like a staircase: a BOS is the next step in the same direction, and a CHOCH is the first step that goes the other way.

formula.name: Breaks of structure
formula.expression: BOS = a close beyond the last confirmed swing in the trend's direction;  CHOCH = the first such close against the trend
formula.spoken: a break of structure is a close past the last confirmed swing in the trend's direction, and a change of character is the first such close against the trend

variables.meaning: a high above the n bars on each side, known n bars later
a low below the n bars on each side, known n bars later
the bar's close, which must pass the swing

formula.assumptions: A close, not a wick, counts as a break; the first break, with no trend yet, counts as a BOS that sets the trend.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
swing highs at bar 2 (103), bar 7 (104.5); swing lows at bar 4 (99.5), bar 9 (97); each confirmed 1 bars later
bar 6 closed at 103.8, above the swing high 103: BOS
bar 8 closed at 98.5, below the swing low 99.5: CHOCH, the first break against the trend
bar 11 closed at 96, below the swing low 97: BOS

quiz.q: Price is in an uptrend and closes below the last swing low for the first time. BOS or CHOCH?
quiz.a: CHOCH: the first break against the trend.

quiz.q: Why can a swing high not be labelled on the bar that makes it?
quiz.a: It needs the next bars to close lower first; labelling earlier uses the future.

quiz.q: In a downtrend, a close below the last swing low is what?
quiz.a: A BOS: structure breaking in the trend's direction.

misconceptions: A CHOCH is not a reversal: it is the first break against the trend, and many fail.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.
The swing size and the time frame change every label, so two traders can mark the same chart differently.

cards.title: Liquidity pools and sweeps
cards.summary: Stops cluster above highs (buy-side) and below lows (sell-side); a sweep runs them and closes back.

levels.beginner: In ICT language, liquidity means resting orders, especially stops. Buy-side liquidity sits above swing highs, where shorts have their stops and breakout buyers their entries; sell-side liquidity sits below swing lows. A sweep is price poking past such a level and closing back inside, as if it went to fill those orders.
levels.intermediate: Defined on bars: a buy-side sweep of a level is a bar whose high is above it and whose close is below it; a sell-side sweep has a low below it and a close above it. Obvious levels such as the previous day's high and low, equal highs or the Asia range are the ones watched. A close beyond the level instead is a break, not a sweep.
levels.expert: Bar data cannot show resting stops: whether orders really sat there is an inference, and a sweep is visible only after the close. Testable rules, such as "a sweep of the previous day low, then a close back above it", can be backtested with costs; CHE runs exactly that test (pdhl-sweep-5m) and journals the result. Selection bias is the trap: remembering the sweeps that reversed and forgetting the ones that kept going.

cards.analogy: A sweep is like a wave that runs up the beach past the line of shells and slides back: it reached for them, then retreated.

formula.name: Sweep of a level
formula.expression: buy-side sweep: high > level and close < level;  sell-side sweep: low < level and close > level
formula.spoken: a buy-side sweep is a bar that trades above the level and closes back below it, and a sell-side sweep trades below it and closes back above it

variables.meaning: a swing high or low, or a session high or low

formula.assumptions: Closed bars only; a close beyond the level is a break, not a sweep.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
bar 2: traded to 100.75, above 100, and closed back at 99.5: a buy-side sweep

quiz.q: Where does buy-side liquidity rest?
quiz.a: Above swing highs, where short sellers keep their stops.

quiz.q: A bar trades to 101 above a 100 high and closes at 99.5. Sweep or break?
quiz.a: A buy-side sweep: it traded above 100 and closed back below it.

quiz.q: Can bar data prove that stops were resting at a level?
quiz.a: No. It shows what price did, not where orders were.

misconceptions: A sweep is not proof of "smart money": the same bar is also explained by ordinary buyers and sellers.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.
Resting orders are not visible in bar data, so "liquidity" here is a hypothesis about them.

cards.title: Fair value gaps
cards.summary: A three-candle gap where bar 1 and bar 3 do not overlap, left by a fast move.

levels.beginner: A fair value gap is a gap inside three candles: in a fast move up, the first candle's high stays below the third candle's low, so the middle candle left a space where price traded only one way. ICT teaching says price often comes back to that space before going on.
levels.intermediate: Bullish FVG: high of bar 1 < low of bar 3, and the gap runs from that high to that low. Bearish FVG: low of bar 1 > high of bar 3. A later bar that trades into the gap has touched it; one that trades through its far side has filled it. The midpoint is often called consequent encroachment.
levels.expert: Gaps are common on small bar sizes, so most are noise; a minimum size, a time window or a structure filter is needed to make a testable rule. Whether a retest leads to continuation is an empirical question that must be answered after costs on untouched data. CHE's fair value gap retest strategy (fvg-retest-5m) is that test on delayed MNQ bars, with every trade journalled.

cards.analogy: A fair value gap is like a stretch of road a car crossed so fast that it left no tyre marks: traders expect it may come back to drive it properly.

formula.name: Three-bar fair value gap
formula.expression: bullish: H₁ < L₃, gap = (H₁, L₃);  bearish: L₁ > H₃, gap = (H₃, L₁)
formula.spoken: a bullish gap is where the high of bar 1 is below the low of bar 3, and a bearish gap where the low of bar 1 is above the high of bar 3

variables.meaning: high and low of the first bar
high and low of the third bar

formula.assumptions: Bars in time order on one time frame; touched means a later bar traded into the gap, filled that it traded through the far side.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
bars 1 to 3: bullish gap from 101 to 102, 1 point, midpoint 101.5; not touched since

quiz.q: Bar 1 has a high of 50 and bar 3 a low of 51.5. Is there a bullish gap, and how big?
quiz.a: Yes, 1.5 points, from 50 to 51.5.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a touched and a filled gap?
quiz.a: Touched: a later bar traded into it. Filled: a later bar traded through its far side.

quiz.q: Does a fair value gap have to be retested?
quiz.a: No. Many are never revisited; only a tested rule says how often.

misconceptions: "Price must fill the gap" is a belief, not a law: many gaps stay open.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.
On small bar sizes gaps are frequent, so most carry no information without a filter.

cards.title: Order blocks
cards.summary: The last opposite candle before a strong move, treated as a zone where large orders may have sat.

levels.beginner: An order block, in ICT teaching, is the last down candle before a strong move up (bullish), or the last up candle before a strong move down (bearish). The idea is that big buyers or sellers left orders there, so price may react when it comes back to that candle's range.
levels.intermediate: To make it a rule: find a displacement candle whose body is at least a chosen size, then the last opposite-coloured candle before it. Its high and low are the block, and the midpoint is the mean threshold. A block counts more, in the teaching, when the displacement also breaks structure or leaves a fair value gap.
levels.expert: There is no single definition: body size, wick or body boundaries, and whether a break of structure is required all change which candle is chosen. A breaker block is a failed block that price closed through. Bar data cannot show the orders the name implies, so "order block" is a label on a candle, and only a backtest with fixed rules, causal data and costs can show whether reactions there beat chance. CHE tests one version (order-block-5m).

cards.analogy: An order block is like footprints in front of a shop that suddenly got busy: you guess the crowd started there, but the prints do not prove who came.

formula.name: Order block zone
formula.expression: block = range of the last opposite candle before a displacement;  mean threshold = (H + L) ÷ 2
formula.spoken: the order block is the range of the last opposite candle before a displacement candle, and the mean threshold is its high plus its low, divided by 2

variables.meaning: a candle whose body is at least the chosen size
high and low of the block candle

formula.assumptions: One of several definitions in use; the displacement size is a choice.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
bar 3 is the displacement: body 4.5 points up, at least 3
the last down candle before it is bar 2: high 100.8, low 98.5
bullish order block 98.5 to 100.8; mean threshold (100.8 + 98.5) ÷ 2 = 99.65

quiz.q: A bullish order block runs from 98.5 to 100.8. What is its mean threshold?
Which candle is a bullish order block?
quiz.a: The last down candle before a strong move up.

quiz.q: What is a breaker block?
quiz.a: A block that failed: price closed through it, and traders then watch it from the other side.

misconceptions: An order block is not a record of institutional orders: bar data cannot show who traded.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.

cards.title: Premium, discount and OTE
cards.summary: The halves of a swing leg, and the 62% to 79% retracement zone ICT calls the optimal trade entry.

levels.beginner: Take a swing from a low to a high. The middle is equilibrium. Above it is the premium half, where ICT teaching prefers to sell; below it the discount half, where it prefers to buy. The optimal trade entry (OTE) is a deeper zone: a 62% to 79% pullback of the leg.
levels.intermediate: Equilibrium = (low + high) ÷ 2. For a leg up, a retracement of r is high − r × (high − low): on a leg from 100 to 200, 62% is 138, 70.5% is 129.5 and 79% is 121, all in discount. For a leg down the levels are measured up from the low instead.
levels.expert: The levels depend completely on which swing high and low you pick, and with hindsight a good-looking pair is easy to find, which is look-ahead bias. Fibonacci ratios have no known physical reason to hold in markets, and studies of retracement levels find little beyond chance once costs are counted. As a testable rule it needs a mechanical swing definition, made only from bars already closed.

cards.analogy: Premium and discount are like the two halves of a price tag's range in a market stall: you like to buy in the cheap half and sell in the dear half.

formula.name: Premium, discount and OTE levels
formula.expression: equilibrium = (L + H) ÷ 2;  leg up: level(r) = H − r × (H − L);  leg down: level(r) = L + r × (H − L);  OTE: r = 0.62 to 0.79
formula.spoken: equilibrium is the low plus the high, divided by 2; on a leg up each retracement level is the high minus the ratio times the leg, and the OTE zone runs from 62 to 79 percent

variables.meaning: the swing low and swing high of the leg

formula.assumptions: The swing pair is a judgement, and the ratios are conventions, not measured edges.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
equilibrium = (100 + 200) ÷ 2 = 150; above it is premium, below it is discount
leg up, retracing down from the high: 62% = 138, 70.5% = 129.5, 79% = 121
130 sits at 30.0% of the leg: discount

quiz.q: A leg runs from 2,000 up to 2,100. Where is equilibrium?
On that leg, where is the 62% retracement?
Price is at 130 on a leg from 100 to 200. Premium or discount?
quiz.a: Discount: it is below the 150 equilibrium.

misconceptions: A retracement level is not support by itself: it is arithmetic on two chosen points.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.
The swing high and low are chosen by judgement; another pair moves every level.

cards.title: Session levels: Asia, London, New York
cards.summary: Highs and lows of each session and of the previous day, which many traders watch.

levels.beginner: Index futures trade almost around the clock, so traders split the day into sessions: Asia in the evening, London overnight and New York in the day. The high and low of each session, and the previous day's high and low, are levels many people watch, so price often reacts or runs stops there.
levels.intermediate: CHE uses New York time: Asia 8 p.m. to midnight, London 2 to 5 a.m., and New York regular hours 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. The CME day runs from 6 p.m. to 5 p.m. the next afternoon, so the previous day high and low come from that whole day. Each level is just the highest high and lowest low of the bars inside the window.
levels.expert: These windows are conventions; ICT killzones, exchange sessions and other teachers use different hours, and daylight saving shifts London and New York against each other for a few weeks each year. A level is common knowledge, so any edge from it is quickly competed away; test reactions at it with fixed windows, closed bars and costs before trusting it.

cards.analogy: Session levels are like the high-water marks on a pier from each tide: the next tide often reaches for them.

formula.name: Session high and low
formula.expression: session high = max(H) and session low = min(L) of the bars inside the window, New York time
formula.spoken: a session's high is the highest high and its low the lowest low of the bars inside its window, in New York time

variables.meaning: Asia 20:00–24:00, London 02:00–05:00, New York 09:30–16:00, New York time

formula.assumptions: Common conventions, not exchange definitions. The previous day is the CME day from 6 p.m. to 5 p.m. New York time.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
CME trading day 2026-10-16 (it opens at 6 p.m. New York the evening before)
New York regular hours: high 115, low 107

quiz.q: In New York time, when does CHE count the London session?
quiz.a: From 2 a.m. to 5 a.m.

quiz.q: When does the CME trading day for Friday start?
quiz.a: At 6 p.m. New York time on Thursday.

quiz.q: Why do session levels matter to many traders?
quiz.a: Because so many watch them, orders and stops gather there.

misconceptions: Session windows are not official: different traders and tools draw them at different hours.
limitations: A discretionary concept with mixed or limited evidence: definitions differ between teachers, the same chart can be labelled more than one way, and no peer-reviewed study shows it is an edge by itself. CHE treats it as a hypothesis to test on recorded trades, never as a reason to trade.
The windows are conventions; a different window gives different levels.

cards.title: Opening range
cards.summary: The high and low of the first minutes after the 9:30 New York open.

levels.beginner: The opening range is the high and low price of the first few minutes after the New York stock market opens at 9:30 a.m. New York time, often the first 15 or 30 minutes. Traders watch whether price breaks out of that range or falls back inside it.
levels.intermediate: It is the highest high and lowest low of the bars that start from 9:30 to 9:30 plus N minutes. With 5-minute bars, a 15-minute range uses the 9:30, 9:35 and 9:40 bars, and it is known only once the 9:40 bar has closed at 9:45. Using it earlier would use data that did not exist yet.
levels.expert: The anchor is 9:30 New York time, which is 13:30 UTC in daylight time and 14:30 UTC in standard time, so code must use the time zone, not a fixed UTC hour. Opening range breakout studies date back decades (Crabel, 1990); later work finds the effect varies by market and period and shrinks after costs. Test the window length, the instrument and the exit rules on data the rule never saw.

cards.analogy: The opening range is like the first few minutes of a football match: it shows which team is pressing, but it does not decide the score.

formula.name: Opening range
formula.expression: OR high = max(H), OR low = min(L) of bars starting from 9:30 to 9:30 + N minutes, New York time
formula.spoken: the opening range high is the highest high and its low the lowest low of the bars that start in the first N minutes after 9:30 New York time
formula.assumptions: Bars are labelled by their start time; the range is final only once its window has closed.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data

quiz.q: With 5-minute bars, which bars make a 15-minute opening range?
quiz.a: The 9:30, 9:35 and 9:40 bars.

quiz.q: In UTC, when is the 9:30 New York open in winter?
quiz.a: 14:30 UTC; in summer it is 13:30 UTC.

quiz.q: When is a 15-minute opening range known?
quiz.a: At 9:45, when the last bar of the window has closed.

misconceptions: A break of the opening range is not a signal by itself: many breaks fail and return inside.
limitations: Evidence for opening range breakouts is mixed and varies by market and period; costs remove much of it.
A fixed UTC hour is wrong for half the year: the anchor must follow New York daylight saving.
