cards.title: VWAP deviation bands and anchoring
cards.summary: Bands at 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations around VWAP, anchored at the 9:30 New York open.

levels.beginner: VWAP is the volume-weighted average price of the session. Deviation bands are lines drawn above and below it at one, two and three standard deviations, where the standard deviation measures how spread out the session's trading has been around VWAP.
levels.intermediate: σ² = Σ volume × (typical price − VWAP)² ÷ Σ volume, so heavy-volume bars count more, like in VWAP itself. Bands are VWAP ± 1σ, 2σ and 3σ. Anchoring decides where the sums start: CHE's session VWAP starts at 9:30 New York time, the regular-hours open, found through the New York time zone so it stays right across daylight saving.
levels.expert: Price does not follow a normal distribution, so "2σ holds 95% of trading" is only a rough guide, and early in a session σ rests on a few bars. Bar typical prices approximate the trade-by-trade values. A futures VWAP from the 6 p.m. CME open, from 9:30, or from an anchored event are different numbers. Bands describe the session so far; fading or buying them is a hypothesis to test.

cards.analogy: VWAP bands are like the lanes on a running track drawn around the average runner: most stay near the middle, but a lane line never stops anyone from crossing it.

formula.name: VWAP bands
formula.expression: VWAP = Σ(TP × V) ÷ ΣV;  σ² = Σ V × (TP − VWAP)² ÷ ΣV;  bands = VWAP ± kσ, k = 1, 2, 3
formula.spoken: the variance is the volume-weighted average of the squared distance of each typical price from VWAP, and the bands are VWAP plus or minus one, two and three standard deviations
formula.assumptions: Summed from the anchor; bar typical prices approximate trade prices.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
σ = √(Σ volume × (typical price − VWAP)² ÷ Σ volume) = 1

quiz.q: VWAP is 101 and σ is 1. Where is the upper 2σ band?
In daylight time, what UTC time is the 9:30 New York anchor?
quiz.a: 13:30 UTC; in standard time it is 14:30 UTC.

quiz.q: Does a touch of the 2σ band mean price will reverse?
quiz.a: No. The bands describe how spread out trading was; they do not predict.

misconceptions: The bands are not a 95% guarantee: market prices have fat tails.
limitations: Bands early in the session rest on very few bars.
Delayed public bars may have partial volume, which changes the weighting.

cards.title: Trade journaling and performance review
cards.summary: Write every trade down, losers included, and review the equity curve and its drawdowns.

levels.beginner: A trade journal records every trade: the setup, entry, stop, target, exit, size, result and why you took it. Losing trades matter as much as winners. Without a journal, memory keeps the good trades and forgets the bad ones, and nothing can be measured.
levels.intermediate: Record the result in dollars and in R, and the costs. Add the results in order to get the equity curve; the largest fall from a peak is the maximum drawdown, in dollars, and divided by that peak, in percent. Starting from $10,000, results of +200, −150, −250, +300 and −100 fall from a $10,200 peak to $9,800: $400, or 3.92%.
levels.expert: A journal is a dataset, so its rules matter: the setup is labelled before the trade, never after; every trade is kept; and the strategy version is recorded, so a rule change starts a new sample. The deepest dollar fall and the deepest percent fall can happen at different points. Review by setup, session and time of day, but beware slicing too finely: with enough slices one will look great by chance.

cards.analogy: A journal is like a pilot's logbook: it is filled in after every flight, the bumpy ones too, so problems show up in the record instead of in memory.

formula.name: Maximum drawdown in dollars and percent
formula.expression: MDD = max over t of (peak up to t − equity at t);  MDD% = max over t of (peak − equity) ÷ peak
formula.spoken: the maximum drawdown is the largest fall from the highest equity so far, and in percent that fall divided by the peak

variables.meaning: starting balance plus the results so far
the highest equity up to t

formula.assumptions: Closed trades in time order; open-trade swings can go deeper.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
largest fall: from the peak $10,200.00 to $9,800.00 = $400.00
largest fall in percent of the peak = 3.92%

quiz.q: From $5,000, results are +500, −1,100 and +200. What is the maximum drawdown?
quiz.a: $1,100: from the $5,500 peak to $4,400, which is 20%.

quiz.q: Why must losing trades be journalled too?
quiz.a: Without them every statistic is biased upward.

quiz.q: When should a trade's setup be labelled?
quiz.a: Before the trade, so the result cannot change the label.

misconceptions: A journal of only the trades you remember is not a record: it is a highlight reel.
limitations: A journal measures the past under one set of conditions; the next period can differ.
Slicing results into many groups finds patterns that are only chance.

cards.title: Strategy evaluation and verdicts
cards.summary: Judge a strategy by expectancy with its interval, profit factor and sample size: good, bad or unsupported.

levels.beginner: To judge a strategy, CHE looks at three things together: how much it makes on an average trade (expectancy), how sure that number is (its range), and how many trades it rests on. With too few trades, or a range that still includes zero, the honest verdict is "unsupported", not good or bad.
levels.intermediate: Expectancy has two equal forms: win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss, and the mean R of all trades. Its 95% range is the mean ± t × s ÷ √n, using Student's t because s is estimated from the same trades. Good needs at least 30 closed trades, a 95% expectancy range wholly above zero, and a profit factor above 1.2 after costs. Bad needs at least 30 trades and either a range wholly below zero, or a mean at or below zero with a profit factor under 1. Anything else is unsupported: too few trades, missing data, or a range that still includes zero.
levels.expert: The t-interval assumes independent trades from one unchanging strategy; real trades cluster, regimes change, and R-multiples are skewed, so the range is approximate and too narrow if the rules were tuned on the same data. Forward paper trades are out of sample by construction; backtest trades are not, unless the rules were frozen first. Judge each strategy version on its own: pooling different rules mixes their results.

cards.analogy: Judging a strategy is like a doctor reading a test with its margin of error: a single number is not a diagnosis until the margin is narrow enough.

formula.name: Expectancy and its t-interval
formula.expression: E = W × avg win − L × avg loss = mean R;  95% range = mean ± t(0.975, n − 1) × s ÷ √n
formula.spoken: expectancy equals the win rate times the average win, minus the loss rate times the average loss, which is the mean R; its range is the mean plus or minus t times the standard deviation, divided by the square root of n

variables.meaning: Student's t for n − 1 degrees of freedom

formula.assumptions: Independent trades from one unchanging strategy; with few or skewed trades the range is approximate.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
form 1: W × average win − L × average loss = 0.5 × 1.875 − 0.5 × 1 = +0.44R
form 2: mean R = 3.5 ÷ 8 = +0.44R; the two forms agree
s = 1.5454R; t for 7 degrees of freedom = 2.3646

quiz.q: A strategy wins 40% at +2R and loses 60% at −1R. What is its expectancy, both ways?
quiz.a: +0.2R: 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1, and the mean of the R-multiples is the same.

quiz.q: Forty trades, a 95% range of −0.1R to +0.5R, profit factor 1.4. Good, bad or unsupported?
quiz.a: Unsupported: the range still includes zero.

quiz.q: Why use Student's t instead of 1.96 for a small sample?
quiz.a: The standard deviation is estimated from the same few trades, so the range must be wider.

misconceptions: A positive average is not a good strategy until its whole range is above zero on enough trades.
limitations: The interval assumes independent trades and one fixed strategy; clustering and regime change make it too narrow.
A verdict on backtest trades is weaker than on forward trades, because the rules may fit the history.

cards.title: How many trades you need
cards.summary: The sample size that pins a win rate to within a chosen margin, such as plus or minus 5 points.
aliases: how many trades do i need

levels.beginner: The more trades you record, the more exactly you know a strategy's win rate. To know it within plus or minus 5 percentage points, about 95% of the time, you need roughly 385 trades; within plus or minus 10 points, about 97. Thirty trades is a minimum, not precision.
levels.intermediate: n = z² × p(1 − p) ÷ margin², rounded up, with z = 1.96 for 95%. When the win rate is unknown, p = 0.5 gives the largest n, the safe choice: 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so 385 trades. Halving the margin needs four times the trades.
levels.expert: This is the normal approximation for one proportion; near 0% or 100%, or for small n, the Wilson interval is more honest, and the real need is higher when trades are not independent. Precision on the win rate is not precision on expectancy: payoffs vary too, so a strategy can need many more trades to show its mean R is above zero.

cards.analogy: It is like a poll before an election: asking 100 people gives a rough idea, and asking 1,000 narrows the margin, but each halving of the margin needs four times the people.

formula.name: Trades for a win-rate margin
formula.expression: n = z² × p(1 − p) ÷ margin², rounded up
formula.spoken: n equals z squared, times p times one minus p, divided by the margin squared, rounded up

variables.meaning: the expected win rate, 0.5 if unknown

formula.assumptions: Normal approximation, independent trades.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
rounded up: 385 trades for a margin of ±5 percentage points

quiz.q: How many trades pin a win rate to ±10 points at 95%, when it is unknown?
How many more trades halve the margin?
quiz.a: Four times as many.

quiz.q: Does a precise win rate prove a positive expectancy?
quiz.a: No. The payoffs vary too, so expectancy needs its own interval.

misconceptions: Thirty trades is not "statistically significant" by itself: it is a floor below which nothing is evidence.
limitations: The normal approximation is rough near 0% or 100% win rates and for small samples.
Correlated trades carry less information, so the real need is higher.

cards.title: Backtesting pitfalls
cards.summary: Look-ahead, survivorship, overfitting and missing costs: the ways a backtest lies.

levels.beginner: A backtest replays rules on old prices. It can look great and still be wrong: if it used information that was not known at the time, tested only markets that survived, was tuned until the past looked good, or left out costs. Each of these makes the past look better than the future will be.
levels.intermediate: Costs are the easiest to measure: net expectancy = gross expectancy − round-trip cost ÷ dollars risked. CHE's assumed MNQ round trip is about $5.50 (spread, slippage, commissions and fees); on a $40 risk that is 0.1375R a trade, enough to turn a +0.15R gross edge into +0.0125R.
levels.expert: Look-ahead hides in details: a signal on a bar's close filled at that same close, an indicator that repaints, a session high used before the session ended. Survivorship removes delisted stocks and expired contracts. Overfitting grows with every variant tried, so the best backtest of many is mostly selection; Bailey and colleagues estimate this as the probability of backtest overfitting. Freeze the rules, then test once on untouched data.

cards.analogy: An overfitted backtest is like a key filed to fit one lock perfectly: it opens that lock and no other.

formula.name: Cost drag in R
formula.expression: net expectancy = gross expectancy − round-trip cost ÷ dollars risked
formula.spoken: net expectancy equals gross expectancy minus the round-trip cost divided by the dollars risked per trade

variables.meaning: spread, slippage, commissions and fees in and out

formula.assumptions: The same cost on every trade; real slippage varies and is worst in fast markets.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data

quiz.q: A strategy makes +0.10R gross, risks $20 a trade and pays $5 a round trip. What is the net?
A signal uses a bar's close and fills at that same close. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Look-ahead: the close is known only when the bar ends, so the fill must come after it.

quiz.q: You tried 200 variants and kept the best. What should you expect going forward?
quiz.a: Worse results: the best of many is partly the luckiest.

misconceptions: A backtest with a high win rate is not evidence until costs, causal data and untouched test data are all in place.
limitations: Even a careful backtest is history: it cannot show a regime that has not happened yet.
Assumed costs are planning numbers, not a broker's schedule.

cards.title: Monte Carlo of trade sequences
cards.summary: Reshuffle or resample recorded trades thousands of times to see the range of equity paths and drawdowns.

levels.beginner: One backtest shows one order of trades, but the same trades could have come in another order. A Monte Carlo simulation shuffles or redraws the trades thousands of times and shows the spread of results: the typical path, a bad path, and how deep the drawdowns could be.
levels.intermediate: Two ways: a reshuffle uses every trade once in a new order, so the final result never changes but the drawdown does; a bootstrap draws trades with replacement, so the final result varies too. Report percentiles, such as the median and the 95th percentile drawdown. A fixed seed makes the run repeatable.
levels.expert: The simulation can only recombine what the record holds: it assumes trades are independent and drawn from an unchanging distribution, so it misses streaks caused by regimes and any loss larger than the worst recorded. With few trades it repeats their luck. Use it to size risk against a drawdown you can bear, not to prove an edge; the mean of a bootstrap is the record's own mean.

cards.analogy: A Monte Carlo is like shuffling a deck you already hold and dealing it many times: you learn how the hands can fall, but no new cards appear.

formula.name: Monte Carlo of trade order
formula.expression: for each path: draw the trades (reshuffle or with replacement), add them in order, keep the final result and the largest peak-to-trough fall; report percentiles
formula.spoken: each path draws the recorded trades in a new order, adds them up and keeps its final result and its largest fall, and the report gives percentiles across all paths
formula.assumptions: Seeded mulberry32 generator; trades independent and drawn from the record itself.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
200 paths of 5 trades, reshuffled from 5 results, seed 7
maximum drawdown: median 2, 95th percentile 3, worst path 3
0.0% of paths ended below the start

quiz.q: In a reshuffle of the same five trades, does the final result change between paths?
quiz.a: No: the same trades add to the same total; only the order, and so the drawdown, changes.

quiz.q: What does a fixed seed give you?
quiz.a: The same simulation every time, so the result can be checked.

quiz.q: Can a Monte Carlo show a loss bigger than any recorded trade?
quiz.a: Not by resampling: it only recombines the trades that were recorded.

misconceptions: A Monte Carlo is not new evidence: it reuses the same trades, so it cannot prove an edge.
limitations: Assumes independent trades from an unchanging distribution; regimes and streaks are missed.
With a small record it repeats that record's luck.

cards.title: Risk of ruin
cards.summary: The chance that a run of losses takes the account down to a level you cannot trade from.

levels.beginner: Risk of ruin is the chance of losing so much that you cannot keep trading. It grows when each trade risks a bigger slice of the account and shrinks when the strategy has a real edge. Even a winning strategy can be ruined by risking too much on each trade.
levels.intermediate: For equal wins and losses of one unit, with win rate p above one half and q = 1 − p, the classic gambler's-ruin answer over an endless run is (q ÷ p) raised to the number of units of room. Winning 55% with 10 losses of room gives (0.45 ÷ 0.55)^10, about 13.4%. For other payoffs CHE runs a seeded Monte Carlo.
levels.expert: The simulation assumes a fixed dollar risk, independent trades and a known, fixed win rate and payoff, none of which hold exactly: estimation error in the win rate alone can multiply the true risk. Fixed-fraction sizing never reaches zero in theory but suffers the same drawdowns in percent. Set "ruin" as the loss limit you would really stop at, not zero, and read the result as a lower bound.

cards.analogy: Risk of ruin is like a boat crossing rough water with low sides: even with a good engine, enough big waves in a row will sink it, so you raise the sides by risking less each trade.

formula.name: Risk of ruin
formula.expression: Monte Carlo: ruined paths ÷ all paths;  equal wins and losses: (q ÷ p)^units
formula.spoken: the risk of ruin is the share of simulated paths that hit the ruin level, and with equal wins and losses the classic answer is q over p, raised to the units of room

variables.meaning: simulated sequences and the generator's seed

formula.assumptions: Fixed dollar risk, independent trades, fixed win rate and payoff, no costs; a lower bound on the real risk.

steps: Educational example, made-up numbers, not market data
1,000 paths of up to 300 trades, seed 7: win 55.0% of the time for +1R, lose 45.0% for −1R, $100.00 a trade
ruin = equity at or below $0.00, starting from $1,000.00: 10 losing trades of room
130 of 1,000 paths were ruined = 13.00%, give or take 2.08% from simulation noise
check, gambler's ruin with an endless horizon: (0.45 ÷ 0.55)^10 = 13.44%

quiz.q: Win rate 60%, equal wins and losses, 5 units of room: what is the classic risk of ruin?
What happens to the risk of ruin when you double the risk per trade?
quiz.a: It rises sharply: the room halves, and the classic formula has the room in the exponent.

quiz.q: With a 50% win rate and equal wins and losses, what is the classic risk of ruin over an endless run?
quiz.a: 100%: without an edge, ruin comes eventually.

misconceptions: A positive expectancy does not make ruin impossible: oversized risk can still end the account.
limitations: Assumes a known, fixed win rate and payoff; estimation error alone can make the real risk far higher.
Costs, slippage and correlated losses are not in the model.
